analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal federal program paying for home and nursing facility care for people with serious disabilities.
analysis.headline: A universal long-term care bill backed by the Senate Majority Leader and 11 Democratic senators got a single subcommittee hearing and died in the Finance Committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new federal entitlement, under a dedicated trust fund, guaranteeing home and community-based care to any U.S. resident who is moderately or severely disabled — help with bathing, dressing, and other daily needs — plus nursing facility coverage, with added respite support for unpaid family caregivers. Financing was required to be progressive, and the bill also set national standards for private long-term care insurance policies and authorized grants for caregiver training and ombudsman programs.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities who need substantial help with daily activities, and the families who currently provide or pay for that care out of pocket. The bill entitled moderately or severely disabled individuals to home-based services (aides, personal assistance, nursing), community-based services like adult day care, and respite care for family caregivers, with nursing facility care added in the program's third year. Low-income recipients would get help with coinsurance and assessment charges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled adults and their family caregivers

how_it_helps.text: Entitles U.S. citizens and resident aliens who are moderately or severely disabled to community care (home health, personal assistance, adult day care, respite) and nursing facility care, as an entitlement under a new title of the Social Security Act.

Sets monthly coverage of 52 hours of community care for moderately disabled individuals and 88 hours for severely disabled individuals, with additional pooled hours for those with greater needs, and lets beneficiaries elect care at home or in a facility.
Creates a Federal Long-Term Care Trust Fund and requires the public program's financing to be progressive in the aggregate, sufficient to cover net costs, and not drawn from any single age group.

Provides assistance to low-income individuals for the 20 percent coinsurance on community and short-term nursing facility care and for assessment charges, and protects resources for people needing long-term nursing facility care.

Sets national standards for private long-term care insurance — guaranteed renewability, limits on premium increases, inflation protection, limits on preexisting-condition exclusions, agent certification, and bans on duplicate sales — and gives such policies the same tax treatment as health insurance.

Authorizes grants to train home care and personal assistance workers, expands long-term care ombudsman programs to investigate complaints, and directs demonstration projects on a prescription drug benefit for long-term care recipients.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a dedicated trust fund financed in a manner required to be progressive (the bill's subject list includes estate and excise taxes). Beneficiaries themselves would pay 20 percent coinsurance on community and short-term nursing facility care and a $25 assessment charge, with low-income assistance available, and long-term nursing facility care would be means-tested, available only once personal resources fall to a protected level. States would have to maintain their existing Medicaid long-term care spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Progressive federal taxes; beneficiaries pay coinsurance

drawbacks.text: Recipients would pay 20 percent coinsurance on community care and short-term nursing facility care, plus a $25 assessment charge, so coverage would not be free even for families already stretched by caregiving costs.

Long-term nursing facility care would be means-tested: it is available only when an individual's resources are at or below a protected level, meaning families would still have to spend down before the program covered an extended nursing home stay.

Benefits phase in slowly: in the first effective year community care covers only 15 percent of the authorized hours, reaching full hours and nursing facility benefits only in the third and fourth years after enactment.

The bill was a major new federal entitlement with an open-ended financing obligation; its progressive funding design implied new taxes, which its critics could reasonably have argued outweighed the coverage gains or would pressure future Congresses to trim benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Long-term care is one of the largest uncovered risks ordinary families face — a few years of nursing home care can erase a lifetime of savings — and this bill would have guaranteed help nationally, with real support for the unpaid family members who provide most of it. The design had genuine gaps: a 20 percent coinsurance, a slow four-year phase-in, hour caps with discretionary allocation of extra hours, and a spend-down requirement for long nursing home stays. The cost side was also real: a new progressive tax stream to fund a large entitlement. On balance this was a substantial, honestly structured expansion of the safety net, though a far more expensive federal commitment than anything Congress has since enacted in this area.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, whose Medicare and Long-Term Care subcommittee held one hearing in June 1992, but the full committee never marked it up or reported it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. George Mitchell, the Senate Majority Leader, introduced the bill on April 9, 1992 with 10 Democratic cosponsors including Sens. Rockefeller, Kennedy, Pryor, Riegle, Mikulski, Simon, Pell, Adams, Burdick, and Glenn.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which controls health entitlement legislation.
On June 23, 1992, the Finance Subcommittee on Medicare and Long-Term Care held hearings on the bill (printed as S.Hrg. 102-1040).
No further action was taken: the bill never received a markup or vote in the full Finance Committee, never reached the Senate floor, and expired with the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, families continued to bear long-term care costs out of pocket or by spending down assets to qualify for Medicaid. Nursing facilities and private long-term care insurers were better off: no new public program competed for their customers, and the industry avoided the bill's prospective payment limits and strict insurance standards.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing homes and long-term care insurers

sides.party_line_note: All 11 Senate sponsors were Democrats and the committee that buried the bill was chaired by a Democrat, so no recorded vote exists to show how the parties lined up.

industries.note: The bill would have paid nursing facilities from a new federal trust fund at set per diem rates, creating a large guaranteed payment stream. It also imposed prospective payment limits, a capital payment cap tied to bed supply, and coinsurance, so facilities gained revenue under tighter federal rate control.

A universal public long-term care program would have competed directly with private policies, shrinking that market. The bill offset part of that by clarifying favorable tax treatment for the policies and imposing industry-wide standards (renewability, premium-increase limits, agent certification) that cleaned up a market known for misleading sales.

industries.industry: Home health and community care agencies
industries.note: Home health agencies and community care agencies meeting participation standards would have become paid providers under the new entitlement, with fee-schedule payments and care-management oversight.

The bill required progressive financing, sufficient each year to cover the program's net costs and not drawn from any single age group; its subject list includes the estate tax and excise taxes, meaning the largest share of the funding burden would have fallen on higher-income households and estates.
